note: a well-formed objective, the baseline both implementations must accept identically
a verifier object with no `kind` names no checker either implementation can route to; both refuse
a verifier that is a bare string rather than an object; both must refuse the same shape
a statement that is whitespace only carries no question to answer; both refuse an empty one
reward=true: `isinstance(reward, bool)` in the retired Python reference read this as one unit of money; both implementations must refuse a boolean rather than coerce it
a negative reward is not a unit count; both refuse rather than wrap it into a huge unsigned value

a reward one past u64::MAX: within the format's signed-128-bit integer bound but outside the unsigned-64-bit unit-of-account bound `conformance/README.md` pins; both must refuse it as a reward rather than truncate

a reward one past i128::MAX, outside the canonical format's own integer bound. This is the exact shape of the divergence the retired Python reference had with arbitrary-precision integers (`conformance/README.md`'s u64 story) one level up: both implementations must refuse at decode, neither may wrap or truncate

confidentiality="": the retired Python reference decoded this (and 0) as *public*, silently downgrading a funder's declared confidentiality class. Both implementations must refuse an unknown class rather than default it
confidentiality=0: the same silent-default bug as the empty string, from the other direction -- a non-string value must be refused, not coerced

"sealed" confidentiality is a real, known class that both implementations refuse on principle: it would pay for an artifact nobody may read, which needs a zero-knowledge proof neither implementation has. Refused as a deliberate policy, not a parse failure -- and both must draw that line identically
an unrecognised confidentiality class must be refused outright rather than guessed at; guessing here would decide disclosure on the submitter's behalf
a `ratchet` that is an array rather than an object; both implementations require an object and must refuse this the same way
`artifact_schema` must be an object when present; both refuse a bare string

record.artifact_schema: a string is not a schema

note: require_signed_submitter="true" (the string): coercing string truthiness here is exactly the kind of divergence that would let one implementation admit unsigned submitters a funder tried to lock out; both must refuse a non-boolean rather than coerce it
a missing required field (`goal`); both implementations refuse the same absence

deadline explicitly null decodes identically to deadline being absent (`records.rs`'s `optional_string`), so both implementations must compute the *same* id here as they would for an objective with no deadline key at all -- proving neither implementation writes a literal null back into the canonical form

the exact key `serde_json`'s arbitrary-precision feature reserves internally. The frozen bug this guards: a decoder built on `serde_json` with that feature on decoded an object shaped like this as a bare *number*, so a plain nested object and a crafted one produced the same bytes under two different values. Both implementations now hand-roll their decoder for exactly this reason, and both must treat this as the one-key object with a string value that it actually is, computing the same id
a real, signed commitment minted by the CLI; both must accept it and agree on its id
a commitment missing its required `hash` field; both refuse the same absence
a nickname submitter (not key-shaped) carrying no signature: Stage-0 behaviour, unauthenticated and unchanged. Both implementations accept it exactly as they always have

a nickname submitter with a signature still attached to the record. The signature authenticates nothing for a name that is not a key, and `records.rs` refuses it rather than silently ignoring it, so it cannot look like authentication it is not -- both implementations must draw this line the same way
a key-shaped submitter (64 lowercase hex, a real ed25519 public key) with no signature at all; both implementations refuse a claimed identity nobody proved

a key-shaped submitter with a signature that does not verify (one byte flipped); both implementations must refuse it identically to a missing one -- the docs deliberately do not distinguish the two failure shapes

the same public key, uppercased. `signed_submitter` requires lowercase exactly, so this reads as an unauthenticated nickname rather than a key -- both implementations must agree it is unsigned-and-fine rather than one of them treating it as the key and demanding a signature
a real, signed claim minted by the CLI, cites: []; both must accept it and agree on its id
cites="abc" (a string, not an array): the retired Python reference iterated the string and decoded three one-letter citations out of it. Both implementations must refuse a non-array `cites` outright
cites containing a number instead of a claim id; both refuse an array whose elements are not strings

the same citation listed twice. Attribution splits credit across a claim's edges, so a duplicated parent would draw double the flow -- paying the citer for one input twice. Both implementations refuse it
artifact is a bare integer rather than an object; both refuse a non-object artifact
artifact is explicitly null; both refuse it the same way they refuse any other non-object artifact
a claim missing its required `nonce`; both refuse the same absence
a real, signed peer record minted by the CLI; both must accept it and agree on its id
a peer identity one character short of 64 hex; unlike a claim's submitter, a peer record's identity has no nickname fallback at all -- both implementations must refuse the malformed length outright

the identity uppercased: a peer record has no nickname path to fall back to, so this is simply an invalid identity rather than an unauthenticated one. Both must refuse it -- the opposite classification from the same mutation on a commitment's submitter

an addr one character past MAX_PEER_ADDR (255); both implementations enforce the same length bound rather than each other's socket-address parser, precisely so the two never disagree over IPv6 bracket forms or leading zeros
an addr containing a literal quote character, which the format refuses outright rather than escaping; both implementations must agree
an empty addr names nowhere to dial; both refuse it
seq=-1: a sequence number is a counter and both implementations refuse a negative one rather than reinterpreting it
seq one past u64::MAX; a record from an arbitrary-precision implementation must be refused rather than silently truncated into a different, smaller sequence number

a peer record with no signature at all. Unlike a claim or commitment, a peer record has no unauthenticated nickname path -- its whole purpose is to authenticate an address, so both implementations require a signature unconditionally
a transport id that is not 64 hex characters; both refuse the malformed length
